passage:
In Gautam's village near Sangli, everyone's idea of investing was the same: gold, or the chit fund run by the man at the bus stand. When his classmate Seema mentioned a 'crop-bond' paying 24 percent a year, Gautam realised he had no idea how to judge it.
So on Sunday, on the slow phone signal at the edge of the sugarcane field, he read the beginner pages on the investor education website run by the market regulator. It took two hours. He kept pausing and saying things aloud to the buffalo, who didn't care.
'Bank deposit, low return, low risk. Shares, more return over years, but they can fall. So if someone promises high return and no risk...' He stopped. 'Then either they're wrong or they're lying.'
The next day he asked Seema one question: 'What happens to the 24 percent if the crop fails?' Seema didn't know. Neither, it turned out, did the person selling it.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel when Seema first mentioned the crop-bond?
qa.a: Unsure and a little uneasy, realising he had no way to judge whether it was good.

qa.q: What else could Gautam learn from the same website next?
qa.a: How to check whether a product or seller is registered, so the next offer can be checked as well as understood.

qa.q: How might Seema feel when Gautam asks about the crop failing?
qa.a: Caught off guard and perhaps a bit embarrassed, then curious, since the seller could not answer either.

grounding: Shows a student reading a regulator's beginner guide, learning that higher returns carry higher risk, and using it to question an offer.

passage:
Hiroshi had saved 200,000 yen from his part-time job at a ramen shop in Osaka, and a senior at his university kept talking about a currency-trading course that 'pays for itself in a month'. Before saying anything, Hiroshi spent three evenings on the beginner pages of the national financial regulator's investor website.
He took notes on his phone and talked them through with Nadia over lunch. 'Look. Savings account: almost nothing, but safe. Index funds: more, over years, with bad years in between. Anything with much higher returns has much higher risk. There's a chart.'
'So the course?'
'They say "high returns, low risk". The guide says those two don't go together.' He laughed. 'Three nights of reading and I can already spot it.'
Nadia nodded. 'Send me the link.'
When the senior asked again, Hiroshi said he'd rather learn slowly first.

qa.a: 200,000 yen from his part-time job at a ramen shop.

qa.q: How does Hiroshi feel after three nights of reading?
qa.a: Pleased and more confident, even amused, now that he can spot the course's false promise.

qa.q: What else could Hiroshi do before putting any savings in?
qa.a: Keep reading about fees and how to check that a firm is registered, and talk to a trusted adult or registered adviser.

qa.q: What does the reading mean for Nadia?
qa.a: Nadia gets a clear example of the risk-and-return idea and wants the link, so the learning spreads.

grounding: Shows a student reading a regulator's beginner guide, learning that higher returns carry higher risk, and seeing through a course's promise.
